clue.text: A case of mixed dates

parts.note: something placed in the wrong period of history is a case of dates muddled together

explanation.surface: Someone has double-booked, or a box of assorted dried fruit has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dates' are not fruit or appointments but historical times mixed up, as with a clock in a Roman play.
explanation.definitionFit: An error of chronology, putting something in a period where it does not belong, is exactly a mixing of dates.

clue.text: Nonplussed, having mislaid the script?

definitions.meaning: bewildered, unable to think what to say
an actor who has lost the text literally cannot find the lines to speak

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means speechless with surprise; read literally, it describes an actor missing the text of the lines.

clue.text: You can count on them

parts.note: the idiom for reliable friends, read literally as things used for counting

explanation.definitionFit: These are counting frames with beads on wires, objects on which sums are literally counted.

clue.text: He built a wall and kept rain out

parts.note: kept means had, as in held on to

indicators.note: out suggests the word rain is put out of order, its letters scattered

explanation.surface: A builder put up a wall to keep the rain off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept rain out' reads like weatherproofing, but 'out' is the anagram signal. The wall is the Roman frontier across northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman emperor ordered the defensive barrier across northern Britain that still bears his name.

clue.text: Maybe first or second row in exam

indicators.note: in places the noise word within the spoken test

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination
a row, a noisy quarrel, is a din

explanation.surface: A student is told which row of seats to take for the exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' is a noisy racket, not a line of seats, and the exam is a spoken one; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers such as first and second, showing position in a series, are ordinal numbers; 'Maybe' marks them as examples.

clue.text: Move west from Wyoming in terrible disgrace

indicators.note: terrible suggests the remaining letters are put into a jumbled state
move tells us to take away the letter that west stands for from the state name

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: Someone driven out of Wyoming heads west in shame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move west from' drops W, leaving YOMING; add IN and 'terrible' rearranges the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignominy is public shame or dishonour, a close synonym for disgrace.

clue.text: Possibly the safest course for non-pedestrians

definitions.text: Possibly the safest course for non-pedestrians

parts.words: Possibly the safest course for non-pedestrians
parts.note: for drivers, keeping to the centre of the carriageway might be safest, and for anyone a moderate course avoids extremes

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means moderate and avoiding extremes, while literally naming the centre of a street where vehicles travel.

clue.text: No roles for dumb blondes, presumably

definitions.text: No roles for dumb blondes, presumably

parts.words: No roles for dumb blondes, presumably
parts.note: dumb is taken literally as mute, so such actors would get no lines to say

explanation.definitionFit: Roles with lines to deliver are what a literally mute performer could never be cast in.

clue.text: An illegal dispatch

parts.note: dispatch here means killing someone, not sending a message

explanation.definitionFit: Murdering a prominent person is a killing, and dispatch is an old word for putting to death.

clue.text: Bill prepared for posting

parts.note: a bill here is a poster made to be stuck up, not an invoice ready for the mail

explanation.definitionFit: A notice or sign put up on a wall is a bill in the sense of a printed poster.

clue.text: Strips study used for revision

parts.note: a den is a small private room, a study

indicators.note: revision suggests the word used is reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A student strips down a used study guide while revising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'study' is a room, not reading, and 'for revision' is the anagram signal rather than exam preparation.
explanation.definitionFit: To denude is to lay bare or strip of covering, so the verb forms match.

clue.text: There's no alibi to put out for the cancellation

indicators.note: put out suggests the letters of the phrase are disturbed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A trial is cancelled because the accused has no alibi to offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ending a law or practice, as with slavery, is its formal cancellation or repeal.

clue.text: Cross-country?

parts.note: not a running race but a country awarded a cross, the George Cross

explanation.definitionFit: The island nation was awarded the George Cross for its wartime endurance and it appears on its flag.

clue.text: The present month, in a way

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Something is happening this month, in some fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the old commercial abbreviation for instant, as in 'your letter of the 5th inst.', meaning this month.
explanation.definitionFit: In business letters the abbreviation for instant means of the current month.

clue.text: One loses one's head getting no permissions to make chimney corners

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: single means one
the first letter of the word for one
OKs are approvals or permissions

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper on being refused permission to build chimney corners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses one's head' takes S off SINGLE, leaving INGLE, an old word for a fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingle is a fireside, and its nook is the snug seat or alcove by a large open hearth.

clue.text: He stands for England

parts.note: not an athlete or candidate but a figure who represents the nation

explanation.definitionFit: The stout farmer in a Union Jack waistcoat is the traditional cartoon personification of England.

clue.text: Experts on the rocks?

parts.note: on the rocks suggests ruin or iced drinks, but here means knowledgeable about stones

explanation.definitionFit: Scientists who study the earth's crust are authorities on rocks and minerals.

clue.text: Inspire about fifty to make changes in speech

indicators.note: about means the word for inspire goes around the numeral

parts.note: to infect is to fill someone with a feeling, to inspire them
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A speechwriter is urged to rework about fifty phrases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'roughly' before fifty, but it puts INFECT around L.
explanation.definitionFit: To inflect is to vary the tone of the voice or alter a word's ending, a change in spoken language.

clue.text: Downtrodden machine worker

parts.note: not an oppressed factory hand but a pedal literally pressed down by the foot to drive a machine

explanation.definitionFit: A foot pedal that drives a sewing machine or lathe is trodden down to make the machine work.

clue.text: Kind of gun with catches reversed

indicators.note: reversed tells us to read the word for catches backwards

parts.note: nets means catches, as fish are caught

explanation.surface: A gun whose safety catches have been put on the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catches' looks like the noun for gun parts but is the verb NETS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sten was a cheap British submachine gun of the Second World War.

clue.text: A bird's dam

parts.note: a swan is a large water bird

explanation.surface: A bird's mother, a dam, as a breeder would call her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dam' suggests an animal's mother, but it is the famous dam on the Nile in Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aswan High Dam holds back the Nile in southern Egypt, a well-known example of a dam.

clue.text: He's not bound to release a spy

parts.note: to free someone is to release them
an agent is a spy

explanation.surface: A captured spy is set loose because nothing ties him to the crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone independent, such as a player out of contract, is not tied to any club or employer.

clue.text: A doctor tours the French battle scene

indicators.note: tours means the doctor's letters go around the French word

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer, a doctor
la is French for the

explanation.surface: A doctor goes on a tour of a French battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tours' suggests the French city but signals the container; the battle scene is in Texas, not France.
explanation.definitionFit: The mission in San Antonio, Texas, was the site of the famous 1836 siege and battle.

clue.text: It may result in a painful admission

definitions.text: It may result in a painful admission

parts.words: It may result in a painful admission
parts.note: an admission sounds like entry to hospital, but here it is a confession extracted by pain

explanation.definitionFit: Inflicting severe pain to force a confession is the purpose of this cruel practice.

clue.text: Top game can be the very devil

definitions.text: Top game can be the very devil

parts.words: Top game can be the very devil
parts.note: a juggling game with a spinning top, tricky to master, whose name comes from the Italian for devil

explanation.definitionFit: This is a toy spun on a string between two sticks, a kind of top, named from the Italian word for devil.

clue.text: 'Arf a mo!

parts.note: a Cockney call to wait half a moment, read literally as a moment divided

explanation.walkthrough: 'Arf a mo' is Cockney for 'half a moment', a plea to wait briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: A split second is a tiny instant of time, as if a moment had been cut in two.
